articles.title: Iran points to Europe’s war role after Italians killed in Kuwait strike
articles.text:
Iran points to Europe’s war role after Italians killed in Kuwait strike | US-Israel war on Iran News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
Kuwait's Liberation Tower is seen near a Kuwaiti flag in Kuwait City, Kuwait [File: Jon Gambrell/AP Photo]
By Maziar Motamedi
Published On 28 Nov 202628 Nov 2026
Tehran, Iran – The deaths of two Italians in Kuwait in an alleged Iranian attack could worsen relations between Iran and the European Union, warn experts.
Antonio Saccoccio, 65, and Emanuele Lo Russo, 36, were working for a European defence company in Kuwait when they were killed in a drone attack on a military site on Thursday.
Iran has officially denied any role in their deaths, calling it a “false flag” operation intended to draw European countries, which have not officially joined the United States and Israel in strikes on Iran, deeper into the conflict.
Riccardo Alcaro, research coordinator and head of the global competition and political risk programme at the Rome-based Istituto Affari Internazionali (IAI), said the reasons why Iran might deny any responsibility for the attack remain unclear.
“Assuming that the drone was launched by an Iraqi pro-Iranian group, the intention would be to degrade Kuwait’s defence capabilities ahead of a possible new confrontation with the US, which Tehran considers very much possible if not likely and hopes it can deter through such actions,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Their insistence on denying responsibility would reflect a dual objective: avoiding being seen as the aggressor while reinforcing the false flag operation narrative, thereby making it easier to challenge the rationale for a possible future US-Israeli attack.”
Divisions
Politically, the deaths could become a sensitive issue in Europe if public opinion starts associating such incidents with the unpopular war launched by the United States and Israel on February 28, crippling energy supplies and driving up prices of gas and petrol worldwide.
Alcaro believes the response from Italy and Europe will be to continue condemning attacks against countries in the region. Countries whose companies operate as contractors at military bases in Kuwait, which has suffered a series of Iranian attacks in recent weeks, will also have to review security protocols for personnel working at sensitive sites, he added.
Advertisement
“Weapon systems, such as the radar that the two Italian nationals were servicing, are highly complex and require continuous technical support, which can probably only be provided by specialised personnel as the case with the Italian Rheinmetall workers shows. This exposes their personnel to these kinds of risks,” he said.
A second narrative coming from state-aligned circles and media in Tehran specifically implicates Ukraine and redirects attention towards Europe’s role in the war – even as Italy and Kuwait accuse Iran.
The deaths follow an attack by Ukraine on two Russian vessels in Libya on Sunday, prompting widespread anger at Kyiv for appearing to drag its war with Moscow into the Middle East theatre.
Foad Izadi, another Tehran-based conservative political commentator, told Al Jazeera that he believes Ukraine was the culprit in a false flag operation.
Izadi, who is an associate professor at the faculty of world studies at the University of Tehran, said European leaders had “the blood of the Iranian people on their hands” for playing a supporting role for US aircraft and operations.
He pointed to statements made by NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte that confirmed up to 5,000 US military sorties originated from European bases in support of Operation Epic Fury between February 28 and mid-April.
Approximately 500 US military flights had taken off from bases in Italy in support of the operation, Rutte said in late June. Italy’s Defence Ministry insisted that it had authorised only routine logistical and technical operations, not combat missions.
Relations between Iran and the EU have nosedived in recent years over a range of issues, including Iran’s contentious nuclear programme and regional influence. The bloc has imposed many sanctions on Iran and considers the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), a major faction in the Iranian political and military establishment, a “terrorist” organisation.
Izadi said he does not expect relations to improve over the coming years, but said the lingering conflict would only hurt European consumers who are now contending with considerably higher gas and other energy prices for winter.
“It is not to Europe’s benefit to be entangled in prolonged energy wars with Russia or Iran,” he said.
Official response
Italy’s Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said military installations were targeted in Kuwait and that the deaths of “technicians” maintaining detection antennae for a Skyguard air defence system were caused by intercepted drone shrapnel.
Advertisement
The official response from Iranian authorities has shifted between blame on other actors and denial. Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs was quick to reject responsibility.
“The incident is suspicious and looks like a precooked recipe for war,” wrote Iran’s chief diplomat Abbas Araghchi on X, adding that he called his Italian and Kuwaiti counterparts to offer condolences.
Brigadier General Abolfazl Shekarchi, Iran’s armed forces spokesman, also issued a stern rejection and said the US and Israel have a history of launching false flag operations to advance their objectives involving Iran. He described the latest accusations against Iran as “a cover for maintaining hostilities and an attempt to increase insecurity in the region”.
State-linked media in Iran also largely reproduced official narratives, including claims of a nefarious covert operation by outside actors.
“False flag during situation of no war, no peace,” wrote the reformist Mardom Salari (rule of the people) newspaper, framing the Kuwait incident within the current precarious status quo.
But some also warned hardline factions in Tehran about the risk of such incident

articles.title: Court rejects Argentina’s request to stop UK oil activity near Falklands
articles.text:
Court rejects Argentina’s request to stop UK oil activity near Falklands | Oil and Gas News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
A general view of a Falkland Islands sign in Port Stanley on November 10, 2026 [File: Dan Kitwood/Getty Images]
By Al Jazeera Staff, AFP and Reuters
Published On 28 Nov 202628 Nov 2026
An international court has rejected Argentina’s request for provisional measures to halt United Kingdom-authorised oil drilling near the Falkland Islands.
Saturday’s ruling by the United Nations-backed International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea is a setback to Buenos Aires’s latest effort to challenge economic activity around the disputed territory.
Recommended Stories list of 4 items
list 1 of 4 What’s the Falklands oil project at the heart of latest UK-Argentina spat?
list 2 of 4 What’s at stake in the renewed tensions over the Falkland Islands?
list 3 of 4 Argentina’s Milei threatens legal action over Falklands oil project
list 4 of 4 10 years after divisive Brexit referendum, UK weighs a ‘Breturn’ to the EUend of list
Argentina’s request marks the latest spat between the two countries, which fought a brief but bitter 74-day war in 1982 over the UK-administered islands in the South Atlantic.
In September, Argentina launched an arbitration process against London over the Sea Lion project off the Falklands, which is led by the UK’s Rockhopper company and Israel’s Navitas.
Buenos Aires has argued the plan violates a UN resolution calling for both sides to desist from unilateral actions until their dispute over the sovereignty of the islands is resolved.
It has asked the court to impose emergency measures and order the UK to take the necessary steps “to ensure that no new drilling for exploitation, and no installation of production infrastructure” takes place in the North Malvinas Basin.
It further urged the Hamburg-based court, an independent court set up under UN auspices, to order the UK to “refrain from using the information obtained in the exploration of the natural resources of the disputed maritime areas”.
The Sea Lion oil field is located about 220km (135 miles) from the islands, which lie 600km (372 miles) off Argentina’s Patagonian coast and almost 13,000km (8,077 miles) from the UK.
Advertisement
Argentinian President Javier Milei has doubled down on his country’s claim over the Falklands – known in Argentina as Las Malvinas – since US President Donald Trump said he was open to reviewing Washington’s stance on the territory.
Reacting to the ruling, he said Buenos Aires will continue its efforts to halt the project.
“This decision is not the final word,” Milei said in a statement, noting that Argentina will continue to “assert its rights through all diplomatic, legal and administrative channels at its disposal.”
The Falkland Islanders themselves voted overwhelmingly in 2013 to remain part of the UK.
But Argentina rejects that outcome, arguing the principle of self-determination does not apply to a population it considers implanted by the UK after 1833.
London’s argument
The UK, meanwhile, has urged the court to reject the case, saying it was rooted in Argentina’s claims to sovereignty.
London argues the sovereignty claim falls outside the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea’s arbitration process aimed at settling maritime disputes.
The UK government’s chief legal adviser, Ellie Reeves, told the judges in a two-day hearing earlier this month that the order sought by Argentina “would prevent the people of the Falkland Islands from developing their natural resources, as they are entitled to do so”.
This could have “devastating” economic consequences for the islanders, she said, adding that what Argentina “wants is to take control of those resources for itself”.
Britain’s Prime Minister Andy Burnham also raised the Sea Lion project with Trump in a call in late October.
“The prime minister raised the economic consequences of Argentina’s coercive measures for the UK and US and reiterated the importance of respecting the islanders’ right to develop their natural resources,” Burnham’s office said in a statement.
The tribunal was set up under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which came into force in 1994 and which sets out a “regime of law and order in the world’s oceans and seas, establishing rules governing all uses of the oceans and their resources”.
If the court orders provisional emergency measures, these would be legally binding on both parties.
Advertisement

articles.title: Two visions of Spain collide as voters weigh PM Sanchez’s record
articles.text:
Two visions of Spain collide as voters weigh PM Sanchez’s record | Elections News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
Spain faces political shift as far right gains ground
By Virginia Pietromarchi
Published On 28 Nov 202628 Nov 2026
Madrid, Spain – Voters in Spain are set to head to the polls in an election that could open the door to the far right entering the country’s national government, half a century after the end of Francisco Franco’s dictatorship.
After a bitter campaign largely focused on housing and immigration, Sunday’s snap vote pits two sharply different accounts of socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s eight years in power against each other. One says the country has become a bastion of social progress and a driver of economic growth in a largely stagnant Europe. The other, embraced by the opposition conservatives and the far right, says Spain needs a profound change after years of alleged corruption and opportunism.
Recommended Stories list of 3 items
list 1 of 3 Police investigating bomb threats against schools in Germany and Denmark
list 2 of 3 Kilmar Abrego Garcia self-deports to Spain after lengthy US legal battle
list 3 of 3 Catalan separatist Puigdemont to return to Spain on December 12end of list
“They [the elections] have been framed in plebiscitary terms, as a vote for or against Pedro Sanchez’s leadership,” Alvaro Sanchez-Garcia, a political scientist and postdoctoral fellow at Spain’s Centre for Political and Constitutional Studies, told Al Jazeera. In a campaign this polarising, he said, voters who switch parties tend to stay within the same bloc, with only a few crossing from left to right or the other way around.
Polls suggest the conservative People’s Party (PP) will win most seats but will need the far-right Vox party – projected to finish third – to secure the 176 seats required for an outright majority in the 350-seat Congress of Deputies. Most surveys suggest the PP and Vox would reach that number together, giving PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo a path to power through either a coalition or a minority government backed by Vox in parliament.
(Al Jazeera)
Despite the unfavourable predictions, Sanchez has expressed optimism that left-leaning voters will mobilise in large numbers come election day to prevent a right-wing surge. In 2023, his PSOE had finished second but Sanchez secured another term with support from parties to his left, and Catalan and Basque groupings.
Advertisement
“I can’t conceive of us losing,” he said in a radio interview on Friday, before addressing supporters at his  final campaign rally in the capital, Madrid: “This election about one thing only: Whether Spain moves forward or goes backwards.”
In power since 2018, Sanchez says Spain has never been in a better shape, pointing to the dynamism of the country’s economy. The European Commission forecasts growth of 2.6 percent for Spain this year, compared with 1.2 percent for the eurozone.
Sanchez has become a popular figure among Europe’s progressives at a time of a wider shift to the right across the European Union. The 54-year-old has frequently clashed with US President Donald Trump, refused to increase defence spending to 5 percent as requested by other NATO members and called Israel’s war in Gaza a genocide.
But at home, not everyone sees him the same way. “People abroad think he is a hero, but not here,” said Isabel Labayen, a longtime PP voter. “How is it possible that we are praised abroad but people [in Spain] can’t afford a house, food or have doctor appointments in months rather than days?” the 64-year-old asked. “We have a problem.”
(Al Jazeera)
Housing was also what brought the election forward. Sanchez called the snap vote in October after parliament rejected two measures intended to protect renters following protests over high housing costs and evictions.
Opponents say Sanchez’s moments on the world stage have failed to translate into better living conditions for people in Spain. “You can’t eat GDP,” Feijoo told the prime minister during a televised debate last week.
Critics also say the economic indicators might have indeed improved, but this was mostly driven by the absorption of foreign labour; the minimum wage has increased, but average salaries have remained the same; and services feel increasingly stretched as foreign-born residents have grown by more than four million since the PSOE took power in 2018.
Sanchez’s reputation has also been tarnished by corruption cases involving his inner circle and family, the handling of a migration crisis in the North African enclave of Ceuta earlier this year and two deadly train crashes a few months apart that provided the opposition with ammunition to attack the government for overseeing a failed state that very much needs repairing.
This has energised Vox, which has become a rising political force in recent years. Campaigning on giving Spaniards “national priority” – a system that would create a two-tier society in which Spanish nationals would have better access to social benefits – and banning mass regularisation of migration, the far-right party is predicted to make the biggest gains compared with the other major parties. In 2023, it secured 33 of the 350 seats in Congress; it is now set to double that, capturing about 18 percent of the national vote.
Advertisement
“We’re governed by a criminal mafia, led by an unscrupulous boss who knows no bounds when it comes to lying,” Vox leader Santiago Abascal told supporters at his last rally, held inside a bullring in Valencia, on Friday.
Feijoo has previously said he would prefer the PP to rule on its own, with Vox supporting it in parliament, rather than forming a joint governing coalition. That will depend on numbers: should the far-right party make major gains, it will have stronger leverage in any negotiations.
Yolanda Roman, the global director for public affairs at ATREVIA, said the prospect of a PP-Vox coalition seems to frighten voters less than it did in 2023. That could make it hard

articles.title: Taiwan opposition party wins re-election in Taipei mayoral race
articles.text:
Taiwan opposition party wins re-election in Taipei mayoral race | Elections News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
People gather to watch election results near the campaign headquarters of Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen in Taipei on November 28, 2026 [Cheng Yu-chen/AFP]
By Al Jazeera Staff and Reuters
Published On 28 Nov 202628 Nov 2026
The candidate for Taiwan’s opposition Kuomintang party (KMT) has secured re-election in the mayoral race for the capital, Taipei, after his main rival conceded defeat.
Voters on Saturday cast ballots for some 11,000 positions across Taiwan’s 16 counties and “six municipalities”, or largest cities, in local elections closely watched by China, which considers the self-ruling island to be a part of its territory and has pledged reunification by force if necessary.
Recommended Stories list of 4 items
list 1 of 4 Taiwan votes in local elections to choose mayors, other leaders
list 2 of 4 Will Taiwan vote to revive nuclear power – and why does that matter for AI?
list 3 of 4 Hong Kong democracy activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in jail
list 4 of 4 ‘Hybrid warfare’: Taiwan drives away 16 Chinese shipsend of list
The DPP looked set to clinch half of the municipalities, taking back Taichung – the island’s second most populous city – along with Tainan and Kaohsiung.
But its Taipei candidate, academic Puma Shen, conceded defeat late on Saturday to incumbent Chiang Wan-an of the KMT. Chiang won by a double-digit margin in the previous election and is seen as a possible future presidential candidate.
In addition to the capital, the KMT is likely to win the other two municipalities: New Taipei City, the most populous of the six municipalities, and Taoyuan.
Election campaigns ahead of the vote centred on domestic issues including transport, childcare and the environment, rather than disputed ties with China.
The KMT traditionally favours closer ties with Beijing, while the ruling DPP rejects China’s sovereignty claims. KMT chairwoman Cheng Li-wun met Chinese President Xi Jinping in April.
Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defence said 33 Chinese warplanes encircled Taiwan on Friday, including bombers and fighter jets, along with eight warships.
Advertisement
The KMT dominated the last local elections, winning across 14 cities and counties. The DPP managed only 5, while other parties and independents took 3.
Preparations and campaigns for the 2028 presidential and parliamentary elections are expected to start after Saturday’s election results.
President William Lai Ching-te of the DPP is likely to run again, while outgoing Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen could be the KMT’s frontrunner.
Advertisement

articles.title: At least 10 students killed in blast beside school in Afghanistan’s Kunar
articles.text:
At least 10 students killed in blast beside school in Afghanistan’s Kunar | News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
Several students killed in blast beside Afghan school
By Al Jazeera Staff
Published On 28 Nov 202628 Nov 2026
At least 10 students have been killed and about 110 injured in an explosion next to a school in the city of Asadabad in eastern Afghanistan’s Kunar province, according to the country’s Ministry of Interior Affairs.
The explosion occurred in a house beside a middle school in the Andar Ser area of Asadabad at about 10am (05:30 GMT) on Saturday, Mawlawi Sami-ul-Haq, the director of information and culture in Kunar, told Al Jazeera.
He said the house belonged to people involved in mining operations who had stored dynamite there.
Mufti Abdul Mateen Qani, the Interior Ministry spokesman, said the explosion occurred due to negligence and carelessness, according to initial investigations.
Afghan schoolchildren and other victims injured in an explosion receive medical treatment at a hospital in Asadabad, in Afghanistan’s Kunar province, on November 28, 2026 [AFP]
Mining is a key industry in Afghanistan, a country rich in raw materials, including iron ore, copper, lead, zinc, gold, coal and precious stones. But safety standards at the mining companies are often poor, leading to accidents.
Gemstone mining is on the rise in Kunar, with various companies extracting precious stones that are subsequently sold at auction.
In August, a hand grenade attack at a school complex in the Afghan capital of Kabul wounded more than 40 children aged between nine and 14.
[Al Jazeera]

articles.title: Israeli ‘direct hit ‘on Doctors Without Borders Gaza clinic kills 2 staff
articles.text:
Israeli ‘direct hit ‘on Doctors Without Borders Gaza clinic kills 2 staff | Israel-Palestine conflict News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
A member of the Palestinian Civil Defence douses the flames on a car hit in an Israeli strike on Gaza City on November 23, 2026 [Omar Al Qattaa/AFP]
By Al Jazeera Staff
Published On 28 Nov 202628 Nov 2026
Two staff members of Doctors Without Borders, the humanitarian relief agency known by its French initials MSF, have been killed in an Israeli strike on one of its clinics in Gaza City.
“We are devastated and outraged by the killing of two of our colleagues, both watchmen, in an Israeli strike on one of our Gaza clinics tonight,” MSF said on X on Friday.
Recommended Stories list of 3 items
list 1 of 3 Kushner explains the ‘good thing’ about Gaza’s destruction
list 2 of 3 Israeli attacks on women and girls meant ‘to destroy life’ in Gaza: Amnesty
list 3 of 3 Israel kills four in Gaza as Hamas chief al-Hayya’s son survives strikeend of list
It called the attack a “direct hit” and said the killings bring the number of its staff killed in Gaza to 17.
The agency’s premises were “clearly marked with MSF logos, and their location had been communicated to and was known by the Israeli military”, the group said.
It called for those responsible to be held accountable.
In a statement following the strike, the Israeli military claimed, without providing evidence, that the two workers were members of Hamas.
World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus called the attack “outrageous and unacceptable”.
“Those risking their lives to save others must be protected, not attacked,” he wrote on X.
A pattern of attacks
Israel’s forces have killed more than 1,700 health workers since the start of its genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip in October 2023.
In January, MSF said Israel had blocked its supplies and denied entry to all its international staff since the start of the year.
Israeli officials have alleged, without proof, that aid groups are linked to Hamas, while aid organisations say such accusations have helped normalise attacks on humanitarian workers.
Advertisement
Earlier this week, an Israeli strike in Gaza killed Adel al-Helou, who had worked for 35 years for UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees. Al-Helou was supplying water to residents of the Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza. Three other people were wounded in the attack, UNRWA and medics said.
“Without respite, Israel continues to kill, injure, and decimate Palestinian life throughout Gaza, in plain view of those who have the means, and who the bear the duty to force an end to the genocide,” James Smith, an emergency doctor who has worked in Gaza and former MSF staff, told Al Jazeera.
“These repeated attacks send a clear message – Israel will not allow the Palestinian health system to recover. Its strategy remains total extermination,” said Smith, who is also a lecturer and deputy programme director in humanitarian studies at University College London.
The Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor condemned the “attack on a clearly marked MSF clinic” and accused Israel of “systematic targeting of humanitarian personnel and facilities”.
The attacks come despite a “ceasefire” that took effect in October 2025, which Israel has repeatedly violated. Israeli attacks during this period have killed at least 1,705 people, bringing the overall death toll in the war to at least 74,772, according to the Health Ministry in Gaza.
Saul Takahashi, a former deputy head of office of the United Nations high commissioner for human rights in occupied Palestine, said “there is no way” that the attack was an isolated event.
“It’s part and parcel of the entire campaign of genocide,” he told Al Jazeera.
“From the get-go, from the very beginning, the Israelis announced that they were going to prohibit any kind of humanitarian, or any other kind of aid, from entering Gaza; essentially that they were using starvation and the prohibition of humanitarian aid
as a weapon in their campaign of genocide,” said Takahashi.
Advertisement

articles.title: Yemen government forces hit Houthi positions as UN warns of hunger crisis
articles.text:
Yemen government forces hit Houthi positions as UN warns of hunger crisis | Houthis News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
A man watches a bulldozer remove rubble at the site of a reported air strike on warehouses north of Sanaa, Yemen, on November 26, 2026 [Mohammed al-Mahdi/Reuters]
By Al Jazeera Staff
Published On 28 Nov 202628 Nov 2026
Yemen’s internationally recognised government forces have launched multiple air strikes across Houthi-held territory, with at least 121 Houthis killed or injured over the past day.
Reporting from the capital, Sanaa, Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry said on Saturday that more than six Yemeni governorates were hit overnight by the Saudi-led coalition, which backs the government forces.
Recommended Stories list of 4 items
list 1 of 4 Why are families going hungry in northern Yemen even where food is on sale?
list 2 of 4 Could renewed strikes on Hodeidah port worsen Yemen’s humanitarian crisis?
list 3 of 4 Saudi strike kills ’11 civilians’ in Yemen’s Taiz: Houthi media
list 4 of 4 Famine expect to rise due to global conflict, El Nino, warns UNend of list
“In the capital, Sanaa, 13 people were injured, including three critically, who were rushed to a hospital after a gas station was hit in the Tahrir district. The attack also hit homes and shops,” he said.
The second air attack in Sanaa, according to the Houthis, killed a man and his wife after it hit their home, he added.
He also listed an attack on a fuel station in the district of Bani Matar, on the outskirts of Sanaa, a raid on the southern city of Taiz and five air raids in the strategic city of Mocha, along the Red Sea coastline, which targeted a power station.
The “Dawn of Yemen” government offensive comes as fighting has escalated in Yemen in the past months, with Saudi-led coalition forces ramping up operations against the Houthis.
At least 121 Houthis killed or injured
Military spokesman Colonel Majed al-Nuzaili said earlier on Friday that government forces carried out 726 attacks against Houthi positions in the 24 hours prior, and claimed 121 fighters and commanders were killed or wounded. He added that fighting was ongoing in Ma’rib, al-Jawf, Taiz, Lahij, Shabwah, Midi and al-Dhale areas.
Houthi-affiliated media reported that a Saudi air strike killed 11 civilians, most of them children, in al-Turbah in Taiz governorate.
Advertisement
Al Jazeera could not confirm the death toll, and coalition forces did not comment.
Meanwhile, the government-run Saba news agency reported that Houthi attacks on government locations in Taiz on Saturday also resulted in the death of three civilians, including a 10-year-old boy. Three others, including an infant, were wounded.
Coalition officials added that a Houthi missile launched at Saudi Arabia’s capital Riyadh was intercepted and that Houthi attacks on government positions along the al-Masrakh district front, south of Taiz, were repelled.
The claims and casualties could not be independently verified.
Yemen sinks deeper into hunger crisis
Yemen has been racked by violence since the Iran-backed Houthis seized Sanaa and other parts of the country in 2014, prompting Saudi Arabia to lead a military coalition in support of the internationally recognised government in March 2015.
Fighting between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis resumed in July amid tensions surrounding the US-Israel war on Iran, and after a 2022 ceasefire collapsed.
The renewed violence has worsened an ongoing humanitarian crisis, with thousands displaced and the prices of food, fuel and other necessities soaring.
Aid groups warn the crisis has been deepened by dramatic aid cuts by donors like the United States and other Western countries in the past year.
The World Food Programme and the Food and Agriculture Organization warned on Friday that Yemen is among nations facing the gravest risk of food insecurity, and that hunger is likely to worsen there over the next six months.
About 1.8 million people faced emergency levels of hunger in government-held areas, according to the agencies’ analysis. More than 300,000 people have been newly displaced since the escalation began, mostly in Taiz, Lahij and Aden provinces, the report said.
The encirclement of the city of Taiz has created conditions resembling a siege, it warned, adding that Houthi-held areas were becoming harder to access and monitor, and that the group was holding 73 UN staff.
The Houthis encircled Taiz city in early October.
A UN assessment earlier in February had found 18.3 million people across the country – more than half the population – were in crisis or worse.
Advertisement
